I couldn't open a bug report because the form requires confirmation that the bug exists in the latest stable release. This parallel path is only on main and is not included in pandas 3.0.5, so I couldn't truthfully check that box. I'm reporting it here instead.

I found an issue in the parallel read_csv path when using converters=. On the official 3.1.0.dev0+1870.g27449ca07b nightly, a stateful converter produced different results with mode.max_threads=4 and mode.max_threads=1.

issues.title: ENH: move the postgresql extra from psycopg2 to psycopg 3
issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

`pip install pandas[postgresql]` still installs psycopg2. Current pin on
main, in `[project.optional-dependencies]`:

    postgresql = ['SQLAlchemy>=2.0.42', 'psycopg2>=2.9.10', 'adbc-driver-postgresql>=1.7.0']

After #67968 the SQL user guide names psycopg 3 as the example SQLAlchemy
driver for PostgreSQL, so the packaging and the docs now point at different
generations of the driver. This came up in the review of that PR:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/67968#discussion_r3984002256

I wish `pandas[postgresql]` installed the driver the docs recommend.

### Feature Description

Swap `psycopg2>=2.9.10` for a `psycopg` (3.x) pin with an appropriate
floor, moving the coupled spots together:

- the `postgresql` extra in `pyproject.toml`
- the `all` extra in `pyproject.toml` (same psycopg2 pin today)
- `environment.yml`
- the optional-dependencies table in `doc/source/getting_started/install.rst`
  (lists psycopg2 as the PostgreSQL engine for SQLAlchemy)

The psycopg project describes psycopg2 as fully supported for legacy
applications and recommends psycopg 3 for new projects. One compatibility
question decides the floor and the shape of the change: in SQLAlchemy,
psycopg2 remains the default dialect for bare `postgresql://` URLs, so
replacing the pin changes what a fresh `pandas[postgresql]` install can
connect with unless the engine string is explicit.

### Alternative Solutions

- Ship both drivers in the extra (`psycopg` and `psycopg2`): no breakage
  for users relying on psycopg2 being pulled in, at the cost of a heavier
  install. The two packages coexist and SQLAlchemy picks the dialect from
  the URL scheme.
- Keep psycopg2 and treat the docs recommendation and the extra as
  separate concerns; the user guide already shows both dialect strings
  explicitly.
- Replace psycopg2 with psycopg and accept that bare `postgresql://`
  users must add psycopg2 themselves or move to the explicit
  `postgresql+psycopg` scheme shown in the user guide.

### Additional Context

- Raised by @jbrockmendel  in the review of #67968 (link above).
- psycopg project statement: "Psycopg 2 remains fully supported for legacy
  applications. New projects should use Psycopg 3." (psycopg.org)
- SQLAlchemy 2.0 dialect docs: psycopg2 "remains the default dialect for
  the `postgresql://` dialect series"; psycopg 3 requires the explicit
  `postgresql+psycopg` scheme.
- I run the explicit `postgresql+psycopg` path in production (pipeline
  loading ~46M rows per day into PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB, psycopg 3.3.4
  with SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 against PostgreSQL 17).

issues.title: BUG: mixed int64/float64 Index operations falsely match distinct labels above 2**53
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

integer_label = 2**53 + 1                  # 9007199254740993
float_label = float(2**53)                 # 9007199254740992.0

integer_index = pd.Index([integer_label], dtype="int64")
float_index = pd.Index([float_label], dtype="float64")

print(integer_label == float_label)
print("equals:", integer_index.equals(float_index))

try:
    integer_index.get_loc(float_label)
except KeyError:
    print("get_loc: KeyError")

print("get_indexer:", integer_index.get_indexer(float_index))
print("intersection:", integer_index.intersection(float_index))
print("union:", integer_index.union(float_index))
print("difference:", integer_index.difference(float_index))

values = pd.Series(["payload"], index=integer_index)
print("reindex:")
print(values.reindex(float_index))

left = pd.Series([1], index=integer_index)
right = pd.Series([2], index=float_index)
print("aligned addition:")
print(left + right)


Output on pandas 3.0.5:


False
equals: True
get_loc: KeyError
get_indexer: [0]
intersection: Index([9007199254740993], dtype='int64')
union: Index([9007199254740992.0], dtype='float64')
difference: Index([], dtype='int64')
reindex:
9.007199e+15    payload
dtype: str
aligned addition:
9007199254740993    3
dtype: int64
```

### Issue Description

The two labels are distinct: Python equality returns `False`, and scalar `Index.get_loc` raises `KeyError`. However, `get_indexer` returns `[0]`. False matches also occur in Index set operations, reindexing, and arithmetic alignment.

This is not a case where the original integer has already been lost inside a float. The float label is exactly `2**53`, while the integer label is exactly `2**53 + 1`. They become equal only after the integer Index is cast to `float64` during mixed-dtype reconciliation.

Source inspection identifies more than one relevant path. For mismatched `int64`/`float64` dtypes, `get_indexer` calls `_find_common_type_compat`, casts both operands to `float64`, and then calls `_get_indexer`. This conversion rounds `2**53 + 1` to `2**53`.

Separately, `Index.equals` compares the underlying arrays through `array_equivalent` and returns `True` for these two Index objects. Both `intersection` and `difference` have early-return paths based on `Index.equals`, before their general matching logic. The observed results should therefore not all be attributed solely to `get_indexer`.

The practical consequence is silent association of data with a different label. Large numeric identifiers, transaction numbers, or similar keys can reach this path when one source uses `int64` and another uses `float64`, for example after an import or missing-value-driven conversion.

Related but distinct: #61676 and #66794 concern false matches in `isin`. That path now returns `False` for this pair on current main, while `get_indexer`, set operations, reindexing, and alignment still produce the results above. Merge dtype/precision reports such as #8596 and #61688 concern different APIs.

I found no identical public Issue or PR in searches for the concrete value `9007199254740993`, `2**53`, mixed `int64`/`float64` Index operations, and `get_indexer`. This does not guarantee that no duplicate exists.

Mixed numeric Index operations should not match labels that are unequal before dtype reconciliation. For the example above:

issues.title: BUG: SparseArray-backed Series.any reverses skipna handling for float64 NaN data
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

values = [0.0, np.nan]
dense = pd.Series(values)
sparse = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray(values, fill_value=0.0))
frame = sparse.to_frame("a")

print(sparse.any())
print(sparse.any(skipna=True))
print(dense.any(skipna=True))

print(sparse.any(skipna=False))
print(dense.any(skipna=False))

print(frame.any(skipna=True)["a"])
print(frame.any(skipna=False)["a"])


Output:


True
True
False
False
True
True
False
```

### Issue Description

For `float64` data containing `np.nan`, `Series.any` gives the opposite `skipna` behavior when the Series is backed by a `SparseArray`. `DataFrame.any` shows the same behavior for a single `SparseArray`-backed column with the default `axis=0`. With `skipna=True`, the missing value is retained and makes the result `True`. With `skipna=False`, the missing value is dropped and the result becomes `False`.

This is a silent result difference from an equivalent dense Series. It also affects the default call, because `Series.any()` defaults to `skipna=True`.

The behavior appears to come from the non-skipna-aware branch of `SparseArray._reduce`, which currently selects the original array when `skipna=True` and calls `dropna()` when `skipna=False`:

```python
if skipna:
    arr = self
else:
    arr = self.dropna()
```

Related but distinct work: #65478 concerns `SparseArray.mean` accepting `skipna`, and #68194 adds other SparseArray reductions. Neither appears to cover the reversed `Series.any` results above.

The reversed preprocessing branch appears to date back to commit
`56d8e789155231b04131c6bf4674971ec3f38f95` (#22325, October 13, 2018),
which made `SparseArray` an `ExtensionArray` and added `SparseArray._reduce`.
It is present in the v0.24.0 source and in every sampled release line through
3.0.5, as well as current main. The first release containing it appears to be
pandas 0.24.0.

### Automated tools disclosure

I used OpenAI Codex (GPT-5; reasoning-effort setting not exposed) for English
translation and formatting of this report. I reviewed the final issue text
before submission.

### Expected Behavior

The sparse and dense Series should return the same results:

```text
sparse.any()             -> False
sparse.any(skipna=True)  -> False
sparse.any(skipna=False) -> True
frame.any(skipna=True)   -> False
frame.any(skipna=False)  -> True
```

Equivalently, the non-skipna-aware preprocessing should drop missing values when `skipna=True`, not when it is `False`.

### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> pd.Index(list(pd.RangeIndex(-2, -5, -2))).symmetric_difference(pd.Index([], dtype="int64"))

issues.title: CI: sanitizers environment has no pyarrow, so the read_csv pyarrow string path is never sanitized
issues.body:
The `sanitizers` environment has no pyarrow, so the one CI job that builds with `-Db_sanitize=address,undefined` cannot reach the `read_csv` pyarrow-backed string path at all.

`pixi.toml`:

```toml
sanitizers = { features = ["py313", "numpy", "test-base", "optional-dependencies", "sanitizers"] }
```

`optional-dependencies` does not include pyarrow, and every other test environment lists it as its own feature (`pyarrow22`, `pyarrow23`, `pyarrow24`, `pyarrow`). The only other environment that omits it is `no-pyarrow`, where that is the entire point. `pixi.lock` confirms it: no pyarrow and no libarrow anywhere in the `sanitizers` environment.

The consequence is that `_string_pyarrow_utf8` is dead code in that job. `_string_convert` gates the fast path on `HAS_PYARROW` (`pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx:1545`), and the string tests `importorskip("pyarrow")`, so under the sanitizer both the code and its tests are skipped.

That path is the one most in need of ASAN, because its failure mode is invisible to every other kind of test. It deliberately over-reads each token by up to 32 bytes into reserved slack:

```
cdef enum:
    # Bytes of slack `_string_pyarrow_utf8` reserves past the end of its data
    # buffer so `_copy_token` can round short copies up to a fixed width.
    WILDCOPY_SLACK = 32
```

A wrong `wild_limit` offset, a dropped `+ WILDCOPY_SLACK`, or an undersized capacity clamp produces no wrong values whatsoever — only a heap read outside the object, which is exactly and only what ASAN detects. Concretely: while three separate real memory-sizing bugs were present in this code, four rounds of differential fuzzing against the object path found zero value mismatches. Sanitizer coverage is the only thing that would have caught them, and it is precisely what this environment cannot provide.

Two related gaps in the same vein: `py313-freethreading` and `numpy-nightly` are also pyarrow-free, so the deferred/threaded string path has no free-threading coverage either.

The fix is to add `"pyarrow"` to those feature lists and relock. Worth flagging up front that this may surface pre-existing sanitizer failures elsewhere — pyarrow pulls in a large amount of native code that has never been run in this job — so it is plausibly two steps: turn it on, see what falls out, then decide what to suppress versus fix.

issues.title: BUG: validate_test_dependencies.py is blind to pixi [target.*.dependencies]
issues.body:
`scripts/validate_test_dependencies.py` (pre-commit hook `validate-test-dependencies`) checks that every module gated by `pytest.importorskip` / `td.skip_if_no` is installed in at least one pixi environment that runs the test suite.

`declared_packages` builds that set from `pixi["dependencies"]` plus, per environment, `pixi["feature"][f]["dependencies"]` and `["pypi-dependencies"]`. It never reads the top-level `[target.<platform>.dependencies]` tables. `pixi.toml` has one today:

```toml
[target.win.dependencies]
tzdata = ">=2023.3"
```

So a gate on a platform-scoped dependency gets reported as

```
'tzdata' gates tests with importorskip/skip_if_no, but 'tzdata' is not installed in
any environment that runs the test suite, so these tests never run:
```

which is false as written — it *is* installed, on Windows. There is no such gate on main right now, so this is latent rather than currently firing, but it will fire the moment someone adds one, and the failure mode is a pre-commit hook telling the author something untrue about their own diff.

The underlying warning is still worth having: a Windows-only gate does mean the test is skipped on every Linux and macOS job, which is usually not what the author intended. So the fix is probably not to silence it but to parse the `[target.*.dependencies]` tables and reword — report *which* platforms the gate actually runs on, rather than claiming none. Distinguishing "runs nowhere" from "runs only on win" is the useful signal, and only the first should fail the hook.

No false negatives, only a misleading message on what is arguably a true positive.

issues.title: CI: setup-pixi action's environment input description points at pyproject.toml, but the environments are in pixi.toml
issues.body:
`.github/actions/setup-pixi/action.yml:3-6`:

```yaml
inputs:
  environment:
    description: Pixi environment name in pyproject.toml to use.
    required: true
```

pandas has no pixi configuration in `pyproject.toml` at all — no `[tool.pixi]`, no `[environments]`. Both `setup-pixi` invocations in this same file pass `manifest-path: pixi.toml`, and the `[environments]` table that actually defines `py311`…`py314`, `numpy-nightly`, `pyarrow-nightly`, `minimum-versions`, `doctests`, `typing`, `asv`, `docs-and-web` and the rest lives in `pixi.toml`.

So the one line that tells a reader where to find the legal values for this input sends them to a file that has none. The action's own `description:` on the line above already says "the environments section in pixi.toml".

Fix is one word:

```yaml
    description: Pixi environment name in pixi.toml to use.
```

The string dates to `61f964b10a8` ("CI: Use Pixi in CI unit test environments", GH-63969). Small enough to fold into whatever next touches this file.

issues.title: CI: pixi-version is pinned in three places and dependabot bumps none of them
issues.body:
The pinned pixi version appears in three places, kept in sync only by hand:

```
.github/actions/setup-pixi/action.yml:13   pixi-version: v0.76.2
.github/actions/setup-pixi/action.yml:24   pixi-version: v0.76.2
.github/workflows/update-pixi-lock.yml:28  pixi-version: v0.76.2
```

Nothing links them, and dependabot does not bump them. It only rewrites the action reference: `git show aba3a606311` ("Bump prefix-dev/setup-pixi from 0.10.1 to 0.10.2") updates both `uses: prefix-dev/setup-pixi@...` lines and leaves all three `pixi-version` values untouched. So the pixi bump itself is manual (last done in `cae1cd626f8`, "CI: Update pixi to 0.76.2 + relock"), and editing one site without the others produces no error, no lint failure, and no diff anywhere else.

The two `action.yml` sites are the easy pair to get wrong, because they are the same action taking opposite branches of one condition — line 13 serves every environment except `pyarrow-nightly`, line 24 serves only `pyarrow-nightly`. Bumping one and not the other leaves that job installing under a different pixi than the rest of CI, and it is a job whose failures already tend to get dismissed as upstream nightly breakage.

Missing the third site is worse in kind, since `update-pixi-lock.yml` is what *writes* `pixi.lock`: a lock produced by a different pixi than the one consuming it is how lock-format skew gets committed.

Two ways to fix:

- **Pin once in the action.** Collapse `action.yml`'s two `setup-pixi` invocations into a single expression-driven step — `run-install`, `cache` and `environments` can all be derived from `inputs.environment == 'pyarrow-nightly'` — leaving one pin in the action and one in the relock workflow. This also removes the two mutually exclusive branches a reader currently has to hold in their head. It does depend on setup-pixi input-coercion behavior that isn't documented (an empty `environments` must coerce to unset so `validateInputs`' "Cannot specify environments without running install" doesn't fire), so it needs to be exercised in CI rather than reasoned about.
- **Check instead of dedupe.** Leave the structure alone and add a pre-commit check that the three `pixi-version` values agree, alongside the existing pixi-related scripts in `scripts/`.

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

### Reproducible Example

The existing `axis=1` reduction path for homogeneous ExtensionArray-backed DataFrames concatenates the columns into a one-dimensional array. It then constructs the row labels with:

```python
row_index = np.tile(np.arange(nrows), ncols)
```

This creates one group label for every element in the DataFrame. The flattened values and labels are subsequently passed to `_groupby_op` with `ngroups=nrows`.

For supported nullable masked and Arrow numeric or Boolean arrays, the existing groupby kernels can instead operate on column-major data and mask buffers viewed as `(nrows, ncols)`. The specialized path requires only `ncols` zero-valued group IDs and one group. This retains the kernel and the ordering of columns within each row while avoiding the `nrows * ncols` label allocation.

The optimization applies to `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. Unsupported ExtensionArrays, Arrow subclasses and types, other operations, and empty DataFrames continue to use the existing path. Arrow numeric and Boolean arrays delegate through their corresponding masked representation before the result is reconstructed as an Arrow array. Public behavior is intended to remain unchanged.

The following reproducer uses four nullable integer columns, 100,000 rows, and approximately 10% missing values:

issues.title: PERF: avoid temporary allocations in multi-block DataFrame axis=1 reductions
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

## Reproducible Example

Multi-block `DataFrame` reductions along `axis=1` use the `_reduce_axis1` fast path for operations such as `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. For eligible NumPy-backed blocks, the current implementation still creates a per-block `middle` vector and then allocates another result while combining it with the accumulated reduction.

These intermediate allocations become significant for DataFrames with many rows and several blocks. For a guarded subset of compatible NumPy blocks, the reduction and combine steps can avoid these temporaries while retaining the existing fallback for other block types and configurations.

```python
from timeit import repeat

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


nrows = 1_000_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
df = pd.DataFrame(index=range(nrows))
for i in range(8):
    values = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1, nrows)
    values[i::1000] = np.nan
    df[f"column-{i}"] = values

assert len(df._mgr.blocks) == 8


def best_ms(func):
    return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000


for name in ("sum", "prod", "min", "max"):
    value = best_ms(lambda name=name: getattr(df, name)(axis=1))
    print(f"{name}: {value:.3f} ms")
```

### Reproducible Example

## Summary

Python-backed `StringArray` already stores its values in an object ndarray. However, `duplicated` and `value_counts(dropna=True)` currently perform avoidable allocations before hashing for arrays using `pd.NA`.

The two paths incur this overhead differently:

* `duplicated` already passes the existing backing ndarray through `_ensure_data` (`_ensure_data(arr) is arr._ndarray`), so it does not materialize another object ndarray. Its avoidable allocation is the boolean NA mask created by the generic extension-array path.
* `value_counts(dropna=True)` creates a filtered object-array copy through boolean indexing before hashing.

For Python-backed `StringArray` using `pd.NA`, these allocations can be avoided by operating directly on the existing backing ndarray where the missing-value semantics permit it.

## Proposed change

Use the existing backing ndarray directly when:

* The array is Python-backed.
* Its missing-value sentinel is `pd.NA`.
* For `value_counts`, `dropna=True`.

For `duplicated`, avoid constructing the generic NA mask when the backing ndarray can be hashed directly.

Retain the existing generic paths for other missing-value semantics, `dropna=False`, and other string backends.

This does not change public behavior or results.

## Relation to #14860

This is related to #14860, which tracks improving `value_counts` and `duplicated` performance for string data through string-specific hashing.

This change is narrower. It removes avoidable allocations in the Python-backed `StringArray` dispatch path before hashing:

* A boolean NA mask for `duplicated`.
* A filtered object-array copy for `value_counts(dropna=True)`.

It does not change the underlying hashtable implementation or introduce the general string-specific hashing approach discussed in #14860.

issues.title: BUG: IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__ ignores the struct-level validity bitmap
issues.body:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

st = pa.struct([("left", pa.float64()), ("right", pa.float64())])
arr = pa.array([{"left": 0.0, "right": 1.0}, None], type=st)
pd.IntervalDtype(np.dtype("float64"), "right").__from_arrow__(arr)
# <IntervalArray>
# [(0.0, 1.0], (0.0, 0.0]]
# Length: 2, dtype: interval[float64, right]
```

### Issue Description

The second entry is null in the arrow array but reads back as `(0.0, 0.0]` instead of NA.

`IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` reads only `arr.field("left")` / `arr.field("right")`. pyarrow's `StructArray.field()` does not merge the parent struct's validity bitmap into the child, so a null struct entry whose children are non-null is read as whatever the children hold (typically 0).

This is not reachable from pandas-written data: `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` nulls both the child values and the struct-level bitmap, so `np.asarray(child)` recovers the NaN. Only externally-produced arrow data trips it.

The fix is to apply `arr.is_valid()` (or use `arr.flatten()`, which does apply the parent bitmap) before building the `IntervalArray`.

Found while working on GH-64297.

### Expected Behavior

The second interval is NA.

issues.title: BUG: IntervalArray.__arrow_array__ rejects ExtensionDtype subtypes, and ArrowIntervalType metadata cannot round-trip them
issues.body:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

ser = pd.Series(pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks(pd.date_range("2012", periods=5, tz="Europe/Brussels")))
pa.array(ser)
# TypeError: Conversion to arrow with subtype 'datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]' is not supported
```

### Issue Description

`IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` computes the arrow subtype with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype(self.dtype.subtype)`, which raises for any `ExtensionDtype` subtype — including `DatetimeTZDtype`, which `IntervalArray` otherwise supports.

GH-64297 fixed only the read side (`IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__`), so an interval-with-tz column can now be read from arrow but still cannot be written.

Lifting the restriction is not just a subtype-lookup change: `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_serialize__` stores `str(self.subtype)` and deserializes with `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for `timestamp[us, tz=Europe/Brussels]`. Simply allowing the write produces parquet that fails to read back:

```
ValueError: No type alias for timestamp[us, tz=europe/brussels]
```

So a fix needs a metadata-format change on the registered `pandas.interval` extension type, which has cross-implementation compatibility implications and seems worth its own discussion.

### Expected Behavior

`pa.array(ser)` succeeds for a tz-aware interval subtype, and the result round-trips through parquet back to the same `IntervalDtype`.

issues.title: ENH: Add DataFrame.headtail() to show first and last N rows together
issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

## Problem Description

When inspecting a large DataFrame, it's common to want a quick look at both the beginning and the end of the data at the same time — for example, to sanity-check that a sort, concat, or time-series load looks correct from start to finish. Currently this requires calling `df.head()` and `df.tail()` separately and manually comparing the two outputs, which is a bit clunky, especially in notebooks where each call produces a separate output block.

### Feature Description

## Feature Description

Add a new method, e.g. `DataFrame.headtail(n=5)`, that returns a single DataFrame combining the first `n` and last `n` rows, similar to what `pd.concat([df.head(n), df.tail(n)])` would produce, but as a built-in convenience method. Ideally it would also insert a visual separator (similar to how `describe()` or truncated display uses `...`) to make clear that the middle rows are omitted, rather than implying the rows are contiguous.

Example usage:

```python
df.headtail(5)
```

Possible output:

```
   col1  col2
0     1     a
1     2     b
2     3     c
3     4     d
4     5     e
..  ...   ...
95   96     f
96   97     g
97   98     h
98   99     i
99  100     j
```

### Alternative Solutions

## Alternative Solutions

- Users can already do `pd.concat([df.head(n), df.tail(n)])`, but this doesn't include a visual separator and requires an extra import/call pattern.
- `pd.set_option('display.max_rows', 10)` combined with printing the full DataFrame gives a similar truncated view, but it changes global display state rather than returning a usable object, and doesn't work well outside of print/repr.

### Additional Context

## Additional Context

This would mainly be a display/inspection convenience method, similar in spirit to `head()`/`tail()`/`sample()`, useful for quick EDA on large DataFrames in notebooks and scripts.

issues.title: ENH: include cell location in ExcelWriter warning for values exceeding the 32,767 character limit
issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

The `ExcelWriter._value_with_fmt` method checks whether a cell value exceeds Excel's 32,767-character limit and currently raises the following warning:

`UserWarning: Cell contents too long (<cell value length>), truncated to 32767 characters`

The current warning message does not identify which cell contains the truncated value. As a result, users need to further inspect the DataFrame separately to determine which value(s) exceeded the limit.

It would be useful for the warning to include the destination cell location. Here is the expected warning message:

`UserWarning: Cell contents too long (<cell value length>) at row <row>, column <column>; truncated to 32767 characters`

That message makes the warning directly actionable and make it easier to identify truncated values during Excel export.

### Feature Description

Change the  input parameter `val` of the method `ExcelWriter._value_with_fmt` into the **ExcelCell** instance of `cell`. Further update the method to the following format:

```
def _value_with_fmt(
        self, cell: ExcelCell
    ) -> tuple[
        int | float | bool | str | datetime.datetime | datetime.date, str | None
    ]:
        """
        Convert numpy types to Python types for the Excel writers.

        Parameters
        ----------
        cell : ExcelCell
            Spreadsheet cell data that contains the value to be written into cells

        Returns
        -------
        Tuple with the first element being the converted value and the second
            being an optional format
        """
        fmt = None

        val = cell.val
        if is_integer(val):
            val = int(val)
        elif is_float(val):
            val = float(val)
        elif is_bool(val):
            val = bool(val)
        elif is_decimal(val):
            val = Decimal(val)
        elif isinstance(val, datetime.datetime):
            fmt = self._datetime_format
        elif isinstance(val, datetime.date):
            fmt = self._date_format
        elif isinstance(val, datetime.timedelta):
            val = val.total_seconds() / 86400
            fmt = "0"
        else:
            val = str(val)
            # GH#56954
            # Excel's limitation on cell contents is 32767 characters
            # xref https://support.microsoft.com/en-au/office/excel-specifications-and-limits-1672b34d-7043-467e-8e27-269d656771c3
            if len(val) > 32767:
                warnings.warn(
                    f"Cell contents too long ({len(val)}) in row {cell.row}, column {cell.col};"
                    "truncated to 32767 characters",
                    UserWarning,
                    stacklevel=find_stack_level(),
                )
        return val, fmt
```

Update the **four active** function dependency from `cell.val` to only `cell`.

- `def _make_table_cell(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_odswriter.py
- `def _write_cells_write_only(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_openpyxl.py
- `def _write_cells_normal(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_openpyxl.py
- `def _write_cells(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_xlsxwriter.py


### Alternative Solutions

Users can pre-scan the DataFrame for values exceeding 32,767 characters, but this requires an additional investigation of the data. There is currently no built-in way to obtain the location of the truncated cell from the warning itself.

### Additional Context

issues.title: BUG: zoneinfo transition times causes incorrect localization of some Timestamps on 32 bit platforms
issues.body:
Agent (Claude Opus 5 High)-investigated bug 

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Timestamp("1900-01-01", tz="UTC").tz_convert("US/Eastern")
# 32-bit: Timestamp('1899-12-31 19:03:58-0500', tz='US/Eastern')   <-- wrong
# 64-bit: Timestamp('1899-12-31 19:00:00-0500', tz='US/Eastern')
```

This is due to how we populate the transition times cache for ZoneInfo objects

```python
import pandas as pd
from pandas._libs.tslibs import timezones

# Populate the transition cache for a zoneinfo timezone
pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01", tz="US/Eastern")

trans = timezones.dst_cache["zoneinfo/US/Eastern"][0]
print(trans[:3])
# [-9223372036854775807                    0 -2717650800000000000]
#                                          ^ should be -2**59 * 10**9
```

which is a result of this line

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/973d0af19822d4fc8bd58f986e78c533a16dbb53/pandas/_libs/tslibs/timezones.pyx#L398

leads to this failure progression in `test_on_offset_implementations`

> Every TZif file opens with a "big bang" transition at -2**59 seconds, which does not fit in int64 nanoseconds.

> That multiplication wraps it to exactly 0, because 2**59 * 10**9 is congruent to 0 mod 2**64.

> trans[1] therefore becomes 0 (1970) sitting between the NPY_NAT + 1 sentinel and the first real transition, so the array is unsorted — on every platform and for all 597 bundled zones.

> Localizer searches that array with bisect_right_i8, which assumes sorted input, so its answer depends on the array length since every pivot is derived from n.

> Separately, the POSIX-rule validation calls datetime.fromtimestamp(future_ts + 1, timezone.utc), which routes through the platform time_t and raises OverflowError on 32-bit for every future_ts >= 2**31.

> The except handler discards all 124 post-2038 transitions, so len(trans) is 238 on 32-bit versus 362 on 64-bit.

> With 362 the descent probes index 2 (the 1883 EST transition) and returns -18000s; with 238 it lands exactly on the poisoned 0 and returns deltas[0] = -17762s (LMT), off by 3m58s.

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/cookbook.html#cookbook-sql

(`doc/source/user_guide/cookbook.rst`, section `cookbook.sql`; the driver
notes in `doc/source/user_guide/io.rst` are also psycopg2-only)

### Documentation problem

The SQL documentation and cookbook examples only reference psycopg2:

- The driver list and the `stream_results` note in the user guide SQL
  section mention psycopg2 only.
- The dialect string shown for PostgreSQL engines is the generic
  `postgresql://` form; `postgresql+psycopg` (psycopg 3) appears nowhere
  in the docs.
- The cookbook SQL section has no recipes at all — just a link to the
  `io.sql` docs and a Stack Overflow answer.

Meanwhile psycopg 3 has been the current major version since 2021 and the
recommended driver for new deployments, and the `read_sql` warning for
non-SQLAlchemy DBAPI connections ("Other DBAPI2 objects are not tested.
Please consider using SQLAlchemy.") sends users to SQLAlchemy without
showing the modern dialect string — leading to the common
`postgresql+psycopg2` pitfall. Questions about fast bulk loads to
PostgreSQL (`to_sql` being slow at scale) also recur on Stack Overflow
without a documented cookbook pattern.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Add a `PostgreSQL (psycopg 3)` subsection at the end of the cookbook SQL
section with three small recipes:

1. The recommended connection path: a SQLAlchemy engine on the
   `postgresql+psycopg` dialect.
2. A raw-connection pattern (cursor → `DataFrame`, columns from
   `cursor.description`), noting the `UserWarning` pandas emits for raw
   DBAPI connections.
3. A `COPY`-based bulk-load recipe (staging table + `ON CONFLICT` upsert)
   for writes beyond `to_sql`'s performance envelope.

Compared to the current pointer-plus-link, this gives tested, concrete
patterns for the most common PostgreSQL integration questions. The recipes
come from production usage (an ingestion pipeline loading ~46M daily price
rows into PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB) and have been executed as written
against PostgreSQL 17 with psycopg 3.3.4 / SQLAlchemy 2.0.52.

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import copy

df1 = pd.DataFrame(data={"name": "el1"}, index=pd.RangeIndex(start=0, stop=1, step=1))

df2 = copy.deepcopy(df1)
ser = pd.Series(df1.index, index=df1.index)
ser.at[0] = 1
df2 = df2.set_index(pd.Index(ser.values))

print(df1.index, df1.index.values)
print(df2.index)
print(df1)
print(pd.concat([df1, df2]))
```

### Issue Description

After upgrading to pandas 3 we had this issue where after a concat our first df suddenly had a different index for its elements. But I think the issue here is not concat, though a check there would also be a good idea. The actual issue is that it is possible to modifie the values field of the RangeIndex.

Creating a series of a RangeIndex will use a reference that allows modifying the value without touching the start and stop itself. Leading to a behavior that seems like it is a bug.

```
RangeIndex(start=0, stop=1, step=1) [1]
Index([1], dtype='int64')
  name
0  el1
  name
1  el1
1  el1
```

As shown in the output the RangeIndex has a start of 0 and stop of 1 and therefor should contain value `[0]` but it actually contains value `[1]`.
This would not be that big of an issue if the df1 that uses this range index would show index 1 but it shows index 0.
After a concat the row coming from df1 has index 1.

### Expected Behavior

Two options, first: Modifying the RangeIndex should not be possible (as evident by it not being possible to set values directly) so creating a Series of the index should use a copy and not the values directly.

second: modifying may be accomplished but then should also change start, stop.

-> concat should safeguard against this issue? I do not think this is really required as it seems more like the input to concat is the issue here.

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import re

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

ser = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string()))

# 1. all groups named - works
ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(?P<digit>\d)")

# 2. no group named - ValueError
ser.str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
# ValueError: pat='([ab])(\\d)' must contain a symbolic group name.

# 3. named and unnamed mixed - ArrowInvalid
ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(\d)")
# pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Regular expression contains unnamed groups

# 4. same mixed pattern, but with flags (main only) - silently wrong
ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(\d)", flags=re.IGNORECASE)
#   letter     1
# 0      a  <NA>
# 1      b  <NA>

# every one of these works on object, str and StringDtype:
pd.Series(["a1", "b2"]).str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
pd.Series(["a1", "b2"], dtype="string[pyarrow]").str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
#    0  1
# 0  a  1
# 1  b  2
```

### Issue Description

`ArrowExtensionArray._str_extract` is the only `_str_extract` that requires capture groups to be
named, and `ArrowDtype` is the only dtype routed to it (`StringDtype`, `dtype="string[pyarrow]"`
included, resolves to `ObjectStringArrayMixin._str_extract` via `ArrowStringArray`'s MRO).
`pc.extract_regex` addresses its result struct by field name, so `_str_extract` builds the result
from `compiled.groupindex` alone. Three failures follow:

| pattern | behavior |
| --- | --- |
| all groups named | correct |
| no group named | `ValueError: ... must contain a symbolic group name.` - guard in `_str_extract` |
| named + unnamed mixed | `ArrowInvalid: Regular expression contains unnamed groups` - from the kernel; the guard misses it, `groupindex` being non-empty |
| named + unnamed mixed, with `flags` | **silent data loss**: the `re` fallback iterates `groupindex`, so the unnamed group comes back all-`<NA>` while `_get_group_names` still labels it. `main` only; 3.0.5 raises `NotImplementedError` for non-zero `flags`. |

The last row is the concerning one. A full-shaped DataFrame with a silently empty column.

The accessor rejects only patterns with *zero* capture groups, so one unnamed group is valid as
far as the public API goes - this is a backend-dependent restriction on a dtype-agnostic method,
and undocumented: the docstring's own example extracts an unnamed group into column `0`.

**Related**

- #56268 - reported case 2 (via `read_csv(dtype_backend="pyarrow")`), closed by #56334, the PR
  that implemented `str.extract` for `ArrowDtype`: named groups handled, `ValueError` for the
  rest. Its reproducer still fails verbatim on 3.0.5. Cases 3 and 4 were never reported.
- #53846 - adjacent, `extractall` dtype preservation rather than capture groups.

### Expected Behavior

`.str.extract` should behave identically across dtypes: unnamed groups labelled by position,
named groups by name, and the two mixable - matching `_get_group_names` in the accessor,
which already computes exactly those labels.

```python
ser.str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
#         0       1
# 0       a       1
# 1       b       2

ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(\d)")
#   letter       1
# 0      a       1
# 1      b       2
```

This does not require new machinery. `_str_extract` already has an elementwise `re` fallback
for the cases `pc.extract_regex` cannot serve (`flags`, compiled `re.Pattern`). Routing any
pattern with an unnamed group through that same fallback, and labelling by position rather
than by `groupindex`, resolves all four cases above. Happy to open a PR.

issues.title: BUG: Series.corr returns a finite correlation for exactly constant Series
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def report_correlation(dtype, n):
    x = np.repeat(dtype(1.810), n)
    y = np.repeat(dtype(0.576), n)
    frame = pd.DataFrame({'x': x, 'y': y})

    # The stored data are exactly constant, not merely nearly constant.
    assert np.unique(x).size == 1
    assert np.unique(y).size == 1

    with np.errstate(divide='ignore', invalid='ignore'):
        numpy_corr = np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]

    print(f'\n{dtype.__name__}, N = {n}')
    print('-' * 40)
    print(f'mean error for x: {x.mean() - x[0]:.20g}')
    print(f'mean error for y: {y.mean() - y[0]:.20g}')
    print(f'NumPy corrcoef:       {numpy_corr:.20g}')
    print(f'pandas Series.corr:   {frame.x.corr(frame.y):.20g}')
    print(f'pandas DataFrame.corr:{frame.corr().iloc[0, 1]:.20g}')

for dtype in (np.float64, np.float32):
    for n in (1448, 1372):
        report_correlation(dtype, n)
```

### Issue Description

# Constant columns and spurious Pearson correlation

Pearson correlation is undefined when either input has zero variance, so the mathematically expected result for constant columns is `NaN`. This example shows library calculations that can instead return a finite value because finite-precision mean reductions create artificial centered residuals. In the tested environment, the `float32` cases return the expected `NaN`; this is an observed implementation result, not a general guarantee for all versions or array sizes.

One example for float64:

float64, N = 1448
----------------------------------------
mean error for x: -2.2204460492503130808e-16
mean error for y: -1.1102230246251565404e-16
NumPy corrcoef:       1
**_pandas Series.corr:   1_**
pandas DataFrame.corr:nan

Another example for float32:

float32, N = 1448
----------------------------------------
mean error for x: -3.5762786865234375e-07
mean error for y: 1.1920928955078125e-07
NumPy corrcoef:       nan
**_pandas Series.corr:   nan_**
pandas DataFrame.corr:nan

## Interpretation

For the `float64` cases above, NumPy and `Series.corr` can report `+1`, `-1`, or a value very close to either bound even though the inputs are constant. For example, mean errors with the same sign give positive artificial residuals in both columns; opposite signs give residuals with opposite signs.

These are implementation results, not defined Pearson correlations. `DataFrame.corr` uses a different internal implementation here and returns `NaN`. 

## Scan across sample sizes

This compact scan groups equal combinations of mean errors and reported correlations for `N` from 1000 through 1500.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rows = []
dtype = np.float64

for n in range(1000, 1501):
    x = np.repeat(dtype(1.810), n)
    y = np.repeat(dtype(0.576), n)
    frame = pd.DataFrame({'x': x, 'y': y})

    with np.errstate(divide='ignore', invalid='ignore'):
        numpy_corr = np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]

    rows.append({
        'N': n,
        'mean_error_x': x.mean() - x[0],
        'mean_error_y': y.mean() - y[0],
        'numpy_corr': numpy_corr,
        'series_corr': frame.x.corr(frame.y),
        'dataframe_corr': frame.corr().iloc[0, 1],
    })

results = pd.DataFrame(rows)
group_columns = [
    'mean_error_x', 'mean_error_y', 'numpy_corr', 'series_corr', 'dataframe_corr'
]

with pd.option_context('display.precision', 20):
    display(
        results.groupby(group_columns, dropna=False)
        .agg(count=('N', 'size'), first_N=('N', 'min'), last_N=('N', 'max'))
        .reset_index()
    )
```



### Expected Behavior

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def report_std(dtype, n):
    print(f'\n{dtype.__name__}, N = {n}')
    print('-' * 40)

    for name, value in {'x': 1.810, 'y': 0.576}.items():
        array = np.repeat(dtype(value), n)
        series = pd.Series(array)

        # Every element has exactly the same stored floating-point value.
        assert np.unique(array).size == 1

        print(f'{name}: unique values = {np.unique(array)}')
        print(f'  mean error from stored value: {array.mean() - array[0]:.20g}')
        print(f'  NumPy std (ddof=1):  {array.std(ddof=1):.20g}')
        print(f'  pandas std (ddof=1): {series.std(ddof=1):.20g}')

for dtype in (np.float64, np.float32):
    for n in (1448, 1372):
        report_std(dtype, n)
```

### Issue Description

This minimal reproducible example shows that a NumPy array can contain one exact stored value while a finite-precision reduction produces a **non-zero standard deviation**. The **expected standard deviation** of a constant vector **is zero**.

One example for float64:

float64, N = 1448
----------------------------------------
x: unique values = [1.81]
  mean error from stored value: -2.2204460492503130808e-16
  NumPy std (ddof=1):  2.2212131752186999292e-16
  **_pandas std (ddof=1): 2.2212131752186999292e-16_**

y: unique values = [0.576]
  mean error from stored value: -1.1102230246251565404e-16
  NumPy std (ddof=1):  1.1106065876093499646e-16
  **_pandas std (ddof=1): 1.1106065876093499646e-16_**

Another example for float32:

float32, N = 1448
----------------------------------------
x: unique values = [1.81]
  mean error from stored value: -3.5762786865234375e-07
  NumPy std (ddof=1):  3.5775141782323771622e-07
  **_pandas std (ddof=1): 0_**

y: unique values = [0.576]
  mean error from stored value: 1.1920928955078125e-07
  NumPy std (ddof=1):  1.1925047260774590541e-07
  **_pandas std (ddof=1): 0_**

## Why this happens

The reduction algorithm is the same, but its rounded result can vary with `N`. If the computed mean differs slightly from the one stored value, every centered residual (`x_i - mean`) becomes the same tiny non-zero value; squaring and reducing those residuals yields artificial variance.

In the recorded pandas 3.0.5 environment, `Series.std()` uses pandas' `nanvar` reduction path, which accumulates sums in `float64`. That avoids the observed error for these `float32` examples, but it does not explicitly detect constant data and does not avoid the error for `float64` inputs. The precise reduction path can vary across pandas versions or optional reduction backends.

## One possible optional safeguard

Detect an exactly constant vector before calling either implementation. The NumPy wrapper preserves NumPy's default missing-value semantics. The pandas wrapper follows pandas' default `skipna=True` behavior by inspecting non-missing values. In both cases, `size > ddof` preserves the result for an insufficient sample size.

```python
def pandas_std_with_constant_guard(values, *, ddof=1):
    series = pd.Series(values)
    valid = series.dropna()

    if (
        len(valid) > ddof
        and np.isfinite(valid.to_numpy()).all()
        and valid.nunique() == 1
    ):
        return 0.0
    return series.std(ddof=ddof)

constant = np.repeat(1.810, 1448)

print(pandas_std_with_constant_guard(constant, ddof=1))  # 0.0

```


### Expected Behavior

float64, N = 1448
----------------------------------------
x: unique values = [1.81]
  **_pandas std (ddof=1): 2.2212131752186999292e-16_** **--> Expected value: 0**

from io import StringIO

issues.body:
Copying from my comment at https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62242#issuecomment-5424056917

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

data = "01,02\n02,03"

# reading by default parses as numbers
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=["a", "b"]).dtypes
a    int64
b    int64
dtype: object
# but with dtype dict we can override this to stay as string
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=["a", "b"], dtype={"a": str}).dtypes
a      str
b    int64
dtype: object
# however when using integer key, both columns stay as string
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=[1, 2], dtype={1: str}).dtypes
1    str
2    str
dtype: object
```

It looks like the `1` is both applied as a label and positionally?


---

When column names (manually specified `names=`) are integers, `dtype={...}` dict keys are incorrectly applied both as column labels and as positional indices, so a single item in the dict can cause a conversion of multiple columns.

As a sidenote, with the python engine, this works correctly:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), names=[1, 2], dtype={1: str}, engine="python").dtypes
1      str
2    int64
dtype: object
```
---

This is caused by the code here:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4e54dd017d57ae524f74cee9445750c649633809/pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx#L1742-L1751

where for `i=0, name=1` we find a match by name, and the for column `i=1, name=2` we find a match by position, regardless that the key has a match by name as well

issues.title: ENH: Allow assign() lambdas to optionally receive the target column as a second argument
issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Using the ```df.assign(col_name=lambda df: df[col_name])```method is specially helpful when a user wants to modify and perform operations on multiple columns at once, it provides high readability for these scenarios. 

Most of the times, however, the user wants to perform adjustments on already existing columns, perhaps multiplying or adding it by the value on a different column in a further step within the data pipeline. It would be highly useful, for these scenarios, if the lambda function would accept a different parameter that would return the column the user wants to modify as a series. 

This could significantly improve readability, specially when the operations the user wants to perform on the columns are simple, the column names are already long, and rewriting the column name all over again or assigning the col name to a variable earlier within the code would be less convenient.

### Feature Description

The feature could be of great help for users within the specific situations:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"extremely_long_col_name_as_you_can_see": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
     "shorter_col_name": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]}
)

# User later on wants to perform operations on the first column, nowadays this is necessary for doing so.
df = df.assign(extremely_long_col_name_as_you_can_see=lambda df: df["extremely_long_col_name_as_you_can_see"] ...)

# Or perhaps
col_name = "extremely_long_col_name_as_you_can_see"
df = df.assign(**{col_name: lambda df: df[col_name] ...})

# It'd be better if it was possible to do this
df = df.assign(extremely_long_col_name_as_you_can_see=lambda df, col: col ...)

# If all the user wants to use is the column instead of any other column, he could just keep the first parameter as an underscore.
# That would increase readability, and it'd be evident how the only data being used to affect the column is within the column itself or other
# variables within the code. Like so:
df = df.assign(extremely_long_col_name_as_you_can_see=lambda _, col: col ...)
```

For situations when there is no such column yet, a new series with the same length as the original DataFrame filled with np.nan values would be created. The user could just use ```... lambda _, col: col.fillna(whatever_value_he_wants)``` to make his life simpler (if he's editing strings he'd just pass some default or empty string there, if it's floats, he could also fill the column up with zeroes).

## Mind you:

- Passing ```lambda df: df ... ``` should still work after the implementation.
- Passing a lambda with more than 2 arguments should still render a failure, the number of parameters will be internally counted.



### Alternative Solutions

Keep the same structure, but in result lose a little bit in readability and flexibility for users of the method. 

### Additional Context

Not really the same, but there is also the implementation of something similar for the df.apply method, where the user can pass a callable with multiple arguments, such as:
```
>>> import pandas as pd                              
>>> s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
>>> subtract_custom_value = lambda x, custom_value: x - custom_value
>>> s.apply(lambda x: x ** 2)
0    1
1    4
2    9
dtype: int64
>>> s.apply(subtract_custom_value, args=(5,))
0   -4
1   -3
2   -2
dtype: int64
```

print("\n====== gb.indices.items()\n")
for k, v in gb.indices.items():
    print(f"{df.loc[v, "tag"].item():<7} | {tag(*k)}")

# This works as expected
print("\n====== gb.groups.items()\n")
for k, v in gb.groups.items():
    print(f"{df.loc[v, "tag"].item():<7} | {tag(*k)}")
```

### Issue Description

With two or more grouping keys, at least one of them a `Categorical`, and `sort=False`, `observed=False`, `GroupBy.indices` pairs the group labels with the wrong row positions: the labels come out in category order while the row groups are in first-appearance order, and the two are zipped together. `get_group()` is built on `._get_index()` which in turn relies on `.indices`, so it silently returns another group's rows.

`.groups` is computed on a different path and stays correct, so `.groups` and `.indices` disagree for the same `GroupBy` object.

This silently mis-renders seaborn figures. `seaborn/_base.py::VectorPlotter.iter_data` groups with exactly this combination:

```
grouped_data = data.groupby(grouping_vars, sort=False, as_index=False, observed=False)
...
data_subset = grouped_data.get_group(pd_key)
```

So `sns.catplot(..., col=<categorical>, kind="violin"|"strip"|"swarm"|"boxen")` draws each facet's data under another facet's title whenever the facet column's first-appearance order differs from its category order (e.g. any column built with `pd.cut`).

### Expected Behavior

`gb.get_group((0, "low"))` returns the rows whose `g == "low"`, and `gb.indices` agrees with `gb.groups`.

### Reproducible Example

```python

from io import StringIO

import pandas as pd

csv = """id,A,B,C
1,1.5,x,1
2,,x,2
3,2.0,x,3
"""

df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv), dtype={"A": "double[pyarrow]"}, keep_default_na=False)

df["A"] = df["A"].fillna(0)
print(df)
print("isna:", pd.isna(df["A"]).tolist())
```

### Issue Description

Bug in Arrow float conversion: empty strings become IEEE NaN, so fillna does not fill them

When converting string data (e.g. CSV empty fields ,,) to a floating PyArrow dtype, empty strings are not NA (pd.isna("") is False). to_numeric turns them into IEEE NaN, and _from_sequence_of_strings builds pa.array(..., mask=isna(strings)) with that mask all-False. The NaN is stored as a value (null_count=0), not a pyarrow null.

Default pandas 3 semantics treat NaN as NA (is_nan_na() is True), but isna / fillna only look at is_null(). Result: fillna(0) is a no-op.

### Expected Behavior

Empty CSV fields converted to double[pyarrow] should be pyarrow null (<NA>). isna() is True for those rows, and fillna(0) replaces them with 0.0.

### Problem Description

When using `IntervalIndex.from_breaks` one ends up at `IntervalArray._validate` which, among others asserts that the left end of the interval is `<=` to the right end.

At this point an `Exception` is raised so one can assume the the library has completed its task. Hence a slight overhead for a improved error message may be acceptable. Only challenge is to not overcharge the error message, in case there are many offenders.

        if not (left[left_mask] <= right[left_mask]).all():

order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask]

order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask]

issues.title: BUG: test_duplicated_hashtable_impl generates identical codes for every MultiIndex level
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np

n, k = 6, 10

# Current test code: fresh generator instantiated per iteration
codes = [np.random.default_rng(2).choice(n, k * n) for _ in range(3)]

# The arrays have identical values
print(all(np.array_equal(codes[0], code) for code in codes[1:]))  # True

# The MultiIndex built from them has only 6 distinct label tuples
print(len(set(zip(*codes))))                            # 6

# Proposed version: one generator, successive draws
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
codes = [rng.choice(n, k * n) for _ in range(3)]
print(len(set(zip(*codes))))                            # 53
```

### Issue Description

In `test_duplicated_hashtable_impl`, the codes for each level are generated like this:

```Python
codes = [np.random.default_rng(2).choice(n, k * n) for _ in levels]
```

Because `default_rng(2)` is instantiated *inside* the comprehension, a new generator with the same seed is created on every iteration, and *each iteration draws the identical sequence*. As a result, the three levels receive equal-valued code arrays (i.e. they are separate objects, but element-wise they are identical).

Before PR #54209, the test called the shared NumPy RNG once per level. The current behavior deviates from that. Every level's codes match position-by-position, so the MultiIndex collapses to only 6 distinct label tuples. Hence, the current test exercises duplicate detection over a much narrower input than what seems to be intended.

### AI Assistance Disclosure

I found this bug while researching a prospective Ruff rule for detecting repeated RNG resets inside comprehensions. For that work, I'm assisted by OpenAI Codex gpt-5.6-sol xhigh. However, I personally verified the bug and wrote all of the code here myself.

### Expected Behavior

Each level's codes should be a distinct draw from the RNG. We can do this by generating the codes as successive samples from one advancing generator:

```Python
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
codes = [rng.choice(n, k * n) for _ in levels]
```

With the fix, we obtain 53 distinct tuples for the same seed, instead of the 6 tuples returned by the current behavior.

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ser = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-01", "2020-01-02"]).as_unit("ns"))

# plain datetime64 column: correct
ser.to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# '{"0":1577836800,"1":1577923200}'

# behind a Categorical: date_unit is ignored, values written in the categories' own unit
ser.astype("category").to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# '{"0":1577836800000000000,"1":1577923200000000000}'

# same for index labels
pd.Series([1, 2], index=pd.CategoricalIndex(ser)).to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# '{"1577836800000000000":1,"1577923200000000000":2}'

# behind a Sparse dtype: raises
ser.astype(pd.SparseDtype("M8[ns]")).to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values
```


### Issue Description

For `date_format="epoch"`, datetime-like values held behind a dtype that is not itself
`datetime64`/`timedelta64` are not scaled to `date_unit`:

- `Categorical[datetime64]` / `Categorical[timedelta64]` column values, and `CategoricalIndex`
  index or column labels, are written as epoch integers in the *categories'* resolution,
  silently ignoring `date_unit`. The value is off by a factor of 1000-1000000000 rather than
  merely imprecise, so it decodes as a completely different timestamp.
- `Sparse[datetime64]` / `Sparse[timedelta64]` raises `AttributeError` instead of serializing.

`to_json()` converts datetime-likes to `date_unit` up front, gated on `dtype.kind in ["M", "m"]`
and applied with `.dt.as_unit(date_unit)`. `CategoricalDtype.kind` is `"O"`, so categorical
datetimes never enter that branch, and nothing scales them afterwards -- the C encoder's
epoch path assumes the values it receives have already been scaled. `SparseDtype.kind`
reports the *subtype's* kind, so sparse datetimes do enter the branch, and then fail because
there is no `.dt` accessor for them.

The scaling used to happen inside the C encoder (`scaleNanosecToUnit` in
`objToJSON.c::Object_beginTypeContext`), which covered these dtypes because it worked off the
values that actually reached the encoder. GH-63100 cast to nanoseconds in
`DatetimeLikeArrayMixin._values_for_json` to make it correct for non-nano resolutions; GH-63666
then reverted that cast and moved the conversion to the Python pre-pass described above,
removing the C-side scaling. That is where the Categorical and Sparse cases fell through.

Only `date_format="epoch"` is affected -- the `"iso"` path passes the array's own unit into the
C conversion and is correct for all of these dtypes.

### Expected Behavior

Serializing with `date_format="epoch"` should produce the same output whether or not the
datetime-like values sit behind another dtype, i.e. for every `date_unit`:

```python
ser.astype("category").to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit=unit) == \
    ser.to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit=unit)
```

and `Sparse[datetime64]` should serialize rather than raise.

### Installed Versions

<details>

pandas main (3.1.0.dev0), also reproduces on 3.0.x.

</details>

issues.title: BUG: boolean-mask operations on a null-dtype ArrowDtype column abort the process (SIGABRT)
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

ser = pd.Series(pa.array([None, None, None], type=pa.null()), dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.null()))

ser[np.array([True, False, False])] = None   # <- process aborts (SIGABRT)
```

Every one of these aborts the interpreter, all through `ArrowExtensionArray._replace_with_mask`:

```python
ser[np.array([True, False, False])] = None      # boolean-mask setitem
ser.where(np.array([True, False, False]))
ser.mask(np.array([True, False, False]))
ser.combine_first(ser)

df = ser.to_frame("a")
df.loc[np.array([True, False, False]), "a"] = None
```

### Issue Description

For a `null`-typed `ArrowDtype` column, any operation routed through
`ArrowExtensionArray._replace_with_mask` kills the process rather than raising:

```
/arrow/cpp/src/arrow/result.cc:27: Constructed with a non-error status: OK
[1]    79074 abort      python
```

This is a hard abort, not a Python exception, so it cannot be caught and takes down the
interpreter (including a pytest run). It is specific to the `null` type — I swept
`string`, `dictionary`, `int64`, `list`, `struct` and `map` through the same
boolean-mask setitem and all behave correctly.

The root cause is the pyarrow kernel, reduced to:

```python
import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.compute as pc
pc.replace_with_mask(pa.array([None], pa.null()), [True], pa.scalar(None, type=pa.null()))
```

That was reported upstream as https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/47447 and **is fixed,
but the fix is milestoned for pyarrow 25.0.0**. pandas supports pyarrow >= 13.0.0, so with
every released pyarrow this is currently reachable from public pandas APIs.

`_replace_with_mask` already carries a version-independent workaround for the sibling
`replace_with_mask` defect on chunked booleans, immediately above the failing call:

```python
if isinstance(values, pa.ChunkedArray) and pa.types.is_boolean(values.type):
    # GH#52059 replace_with_mask segfaults for chunked array
    # https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/34634
    values = values.combine_chunks()
try:
    return pc.replace_with_mask(values, mask, replacements)
```

so a guard for the null type would sit naturally next to it — an all-null array has nothing
to mask out, so it can simply be returned unchanged. Alternatively it could be gated on the
existing `pa_version_under25p0` flag, which `array.py` already uses for a different pyarrow 25
behavior change.

Noticed while working on GH-64320; the same helper is called from the fix there.

### Expected Behavior

The operations above should return a `null`-dtype result rather than aborting:

```python
>>> ser[np.array([True, False, False])] = None
>>> ser.tolist()
[<NA>, <NA>, <NA>]
```

At minimum pandas should never abort the interpreter for a supported dtype and a documented
API call.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```
commit                : ebd40365c94b2d34ce56ff5bfe1a527ed1bb7f49
python                : 3.13.11
python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Darwin
pandas                : 3.1.0.dev0+1520.gebd40365c94
numpy                 : 2.4.4
dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0
pyarrow               : 23.0.1
pytz                  : 2026.1.post1
```

</details>

issues.title: BUG: tz_localize with a timedelta `nonexistent` silently wraps int64 when the shift leaves the representable range
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2011-03-13 02:30"]).as_unit("ns")  # a nonexistent time in US/Eastern

# shifting past Timestamp.max wraps int64 instead of raising
dti.tz_localize("US/Eastern", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta.max)
# DatetimeIndex(['1718-12-02 02:46:41.145224191-04:56:02'],
#               dtype='datetime64[ns, US/Eastern]', freq=None)

pd.Timestamp("2011-03-13 02:30").as_unit("ns").tz_localize(
    "US/Eastern", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta.max
)
# Timestamp('1718-12-02 02:46:41.145224191-0456', tz='US/Eastern')
```

### Issue Description

When `nonexistent` is a timedelta, `tz_localize` shifts the wall time out of the DST
gap and then converts to UTC using bare int64 arithmetic. If the shifted value falls
outside the representable range the arithmetic wraps silently, so a timestamp roughly
292 years in the future comes back as one roughly 292 years in the past.

`Timedelta.max` is the clearest trigger, but nothing about it is special — any delta
that pushes the result past the bounds does it. Shifting a 2011 timestamp by more than
about 251 years is enough at nanosecond resolution:

```python
dti.tz_localize("US/Eastern", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=100_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['1700-06-07 02:59:24.290448384-04:56:02'], ...)   # should be ~2284
```

Smaller deltas are unaffected:

```python
dti.tz_localize("US/Eastern", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=1))
# DatetimeIndex(['2011-03-14 03:30:00-04:00'], ...)               # correct
```

Every *other* out-of-range shift in `tz_localize` reports itself properly. Both of
these raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime`, so the `nonexistent`-shift path is the one
remaining inconsistency:

```python
pd.Timestamp("2262-04-11 21:47:16.854775807").tz_localize("America/New_York")
# OutOfBoundsDatetime: Converting ... overflows past 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807

pd.DatetimeIndex(["2262-04-11 21:47:16.854775807"]).tz_localize("Etc/GMT+5")
# OutOfBoundsDatetime: Converting ... overflows past 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807
```

The affected arithmetic is the `nonexistent`-shift block in
`pandas/_libs/tslibs/tzconversion.pyx` (`tz_localize_to_utc`), which computes
`new_local` and `new_local - delta` directly rather than going through the
`checked_add` / `checked_sub` helpers that the surrounding paths use.

Related: GH-66550 covered the same class of unrepresentable-UTC-value bugs in the
neighbouring code paths; this block was not part of it.

### Expected Behavior

Raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime`, consistent with every other shift in `tz_localize` whose
result leaves the representable range:

```python
dti.tz_localize("US/Eastern", nonexistent=pd.Timedelta.max)
# OutOfBoundsDatetime: Converting ... overflows past 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807
```

### Installed Versions

Reproduced on `main` at `ebd40365c94` (3.1.0.dev0), Python 3.13.11, macOS arm64.
The bare arithmetic in this block predates the current release, so it is not a
regression.

issues.title: API: astype to CategoricalDtype matches by lookup instead of casting, so legitimate casts silently become NaN
issues.body:
`astype` to a `CategoricalDtype` resolves values by *lookup* rather than by *cast*: `Categorical.__init__` ends up in `_get_codes_for_values`, which does `categories.get_indexer_for(values)`. When the values are perfectly representable in `categories.dtype` but are currently stored in a different dtype, every lookup misses and the result is silently all-NaN.

### Reproducible Example

No pyarrow, no datetimes — just int values against string categories, and vice versa:

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([1, 2]).astype(pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index(["1", "2"], dtype="str")))
# 0    NaN
# 1    NaN
# dtype: category
# Categories (2, str): ['1', '2']

# the two-step cast, which is what was meant:
pd.Categorical(pd.Series([1, 2]).astype("str"),
               dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index(["1", "2"], dtype="str")))
# ['1', '2']
# Categories (2, str): ['1', '2']
```

```python
pd.Series(np.array(["1", "2"], dtype=object)).astype(pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index([1, 2])))
# 0    NaN
# 1    NaN
# dtype: category
# Categories (2, int64): [1, 2]
```

Both emit `Pandas4Warning: Constructing a Categorical with a dtype and values containing non-null entries not in that dtype's categories is deprecated and will raise in a future version.` — but the values *are* in the categories. Only the dtype differs.

### Why this needs a decision now

The deprecation added in GH-62142 will turn all of these into a hard error. Its two motivating issues, GH-40996 and GH-59899, are both about values that are *genuinely absent* from the categories (`pd.Categorical(["foo"], dtype=ci.dtype)`, `"c"` against `["a", "b"]`), and raising there is clearly right.

But the same warning also covers the dtype-mismatch cases above, where nothing is absent. When it is enforced, `pd.Series([1, 2]).astype(pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index(["1", "2"])))` will raise, with a message pointing at the wrong cause.

### Scope

Sweeping 10 value dtypes × 5 category dtypes, comparing one-step `astype(CategoricalDtype(cats))` against two-step `astype(cats.dtype)` + `Categorical(...)`. On `3.1.0.dev0+1520.gebd40365c94` / pyarrow 23.0.1: **50 combos — 25 agree, 11 group A (two-step succeeds, one-step silently all-NaN), 14 group B (two-step raises, one-step silently all-NaN).**

<details>
<summary>Script</summary>

```python

import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

import pandas as pd
from pandas.errors import Pandas4Warning

VALUES = {
    "object[str]":        np.array(["2017-01-01", "2018-01-01"], dtype=object),
    "str":                pd.array(["2017-01-01", "2018-01-01"], dtype="str"),
    "ArrowDtype[string]": pd.array(["2017-01-01", "2018-01-01"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string())),
    "date32[pyarrow]":    pd.array(["2017-01-01", "2018-01-01"], dtype="date32[day][pyarrow]"),
    "object[intstr]":     np.array(["1", "2"], dtype=object),
    "str[intstr]":        pd.array(["1", "2"], dtype="str"),
    "int64":              np.array([1, 2]),
    "Int64":              pd.array([1, 2], dtype="Int64"),
    "int64[pyarrow]":     pd.array([1, 2], dtype="int64[pyarrow]"),
    "float64":            np.array([1.0, 2.0]),
}

CATEGORIES = {
    "M8[s]":   pd.Index(["2017-01-01", "2018-01-01"], dtype="M8[s]"),
